content: The studies reviewed provide detailed insights into the efficacy and safety of direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for treating chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in children and adolescents across different age groups. 1. Young Children (3–5 years): A total of 167 young children were included in seven studies. Sustained virologic response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12) was achieved in 95% of cases (95% CI: 89–99%), with no evidence of heterogeneity. Efficacy rates varied by regimen: 83% for sofosbuvir + velpatasvir (SOF + VEL), 92% for glecaprevir + pibrentasvir (GLC + PIB), and 92–100% for other regimens. No data were available for SOF + daclatasvir (DCV). Among the SOF + VEL group, seven of 41 children experienced virologic failure. One child discontinued treatment due to adverse events (decreased appetite, increased hyperactivity, and spitting up the study drug), while others discontinued due to difficulties in taking oral medication. Discontinuation rates were low, with only 4% of children (5 of 148) stopping treatment prematurely. 2. Older Children (6–11 years): A total of 472 older children were included in 13 studies. The SVR12 rate was 99% (95% CI: 97–100%), with no significant heterogeneity. Efficacy rates were 100% for SOF + DCV, 93% for SOF + VEL, 96% for GLC + PIB, and 99–100% for other regimens. Stratified analyses showed no differences in efficacy rates. Discontinuation was rare, occurring in only 1% of cases (4 of 490 children). Reasons for discontinuation included adverse events such as drug-related rash and severe headache, as well as difficulties in taking the medication. 3. Adolescents (12–18 years): A total of 1,891 adolescents were included in 35 studies. The SVR12 rate was 99% (95% CI: 98–100%), with minimal heterogeneity. Efficacy rates were high across all regimens, with the lowest reported in a small group of six adolescents treated with SOF + DCV for 24 weeks. Discontinuation rates were extremely low, and no virologic failures were reported among adolescents with HIV-HCV coinfection. Both coinfected adolescents maintained HIV viral suppression and achieved SVR12. Adverse events were not reported separately for coinfected adolescents, and no significant differences in quality of life outcomes were noted. 4. Regimen-Specific Observations: Across all age groups, regimens without ribavirin (RBV) were predominantly used, and most patients were non-cirrhotic. Mixed HCV genotypes were common, with genotype 3 (GT3) being less frequently observed in younger children compared to older children and adolescents. Treatment durations were typically 12 weeks, with some variations depending on the regimen and patient factors. 5. Safety and Adverse Events: Adverse events leading to discontinuation were uncommon but included issues such as abnormal drug taste, rash, decreased appetite, hyperactivity, and severe headache. Serious adverse events were rare, with one case of auditory hallucinations reported in a six-year-old girl treated with SOF + VEL. 6. HIV-HCV Coinfection: Limited data were available on adolescents with HIV-HCV coinfection. Two adolescents treated with GLC + PIB or SOF + LDV/RBV achieved SVR12 without virologic failure or treatment discontinuation. In conclusion, DAAs demonstrate high efficacy and safety in treating chronic HCV infection in children and adolescents, with SVR12 rates exceeding 95% across most regimens and age groups. Discontinuation rates are low, and adverse events are generally mild and manageable. These findings support the use of DAAs as a highly effective treatment option for pediatric HCV infection.
